name: Poltergeist Pinnacle
approach: Drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east from Glacier about 12.5 miles and turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), following it about 5 miles to the trailhead at its end; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, drop into the Chilliwack River valley and cross the river, then climb onto Easy Ridge and follow its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, and climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, roughly 16 miles and a full day from the car. From Perfect Pass, rope up, traverse around the Challenger Arm and cross about three miles of the crevassed Challenger Glacier to the base of the pinnacle. This is a genuine multi-day glacier expedition into one of the most remote, weather-exposed corners of the North Cascades, with essentially no bailout options once committed.
descent: Traverse the ridge crest north to Mount Challenger's true summit, then descend the standard Challenger Glacier route back to Perfect Pass.

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. Walk-up only and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. Important: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead and hike roughly 16 mi via Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River ford, Easy Ridge, and the Imperfect Impasse to camp at Perfect Pass (a full day; ~7,000 ft of gain). Day 2: Rope up and cross the Challenger Glacier to the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle (roughly 3 hours from camp per the first-ascent account), climb the East Face route (3 technical pitches plus ~800 ft of simul-climbed ridge), traverse to Mount Challenger's summit, and descend the Challenger Glacier back to Perfect Pass camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.

name: Ptarmigan Traverse
approach: The standard start is the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount. A well-maintained trail switchbacks 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft); the traverse proper begins there, leaving the trail southward across heather and talus toward the Cache Glacier and the notch of Cache Col, where parties rope up. Everything beyond the pass is off-trail alpine travel. This is a point-to-point traverse: the southern exit is the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road near Darrington, so most parties set a car shuttle or arrange a pickup; an out-and-back from Cascade Pass is the common alternative when the Suiattle side is washed out.
descent: The traverse terminates at Downey Creek drainage in the south (elevation ~1,480 ft, coordinates 48.25875, -121.22311). From Itswoot Ridge or Cub Lake area, descend via Bachelor Creek canyon following use trail through burned forest (2020 wildfire recovery) with log-hopping sections to reach Downey Creek Trailhead. An established trail (Trail 768) provides exit through maintained forest. Note: the Suiattle River Road approach (accessed via Darrington-Suiattle Road) was severely damaged by winter storms of 2025/2026; verify access conditions before planning a full north-to-south traverse.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: Planned camp, and the standard first night on the traverse — the first place with water and flat ground after Cache Col. Sites sit on the lip of a steep slope that drops thousands of feet toward the valley, so pitch back from the edge in wind. The col above holds snow well into July and there is no water at the col itself, so parties crossing late in the day carry water up or drop to this lake. Goats work the camp for salt; keep gear and urine spots away from tents. The national park boundary runs at Cache Col just above; camps from here south are commonly described as lying in the wilderness outside the park where no camping permit is required, but confirm the zone with the ranger station when you pick up your trailhead permit.
bivy.water: the lake, and snowmelt runnels feeding it
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: Planned camp, the usual second night, in heather meadow among granite boulders below the Le Conte Glacier. It is a low point on the traverse and melts out later than its elevation suggests — a party in late June found nothing bare and pitched on snow with running water alongside. Sheltered relative to the passes on either side, but the basin is a cold sink. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes; flowing water available even under snow cover
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: Planned camp, the last true alpine camp and the one most parties would not skip, looking straight across at the icefalls of Dome and Sinister. Dry dirt bivy platforms are usable by late June, earlier than the lower camps. It is an open basin with nothing to hide behind: one party sat out roughly twelve hours of rain and wind in tents here, so anchor well and pick a site with a boulder on the windward side. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes
bivy.capacity: at least three good sites; more on snow

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows / Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned camp, the last night for parties exiting south to Downey Creek, in heather meadow below Itswoot Ridge. Melts out late — a late-June party found the lake still largely frozen, the basin barely opened up, and a marginal perch near 6,200 ft below the basin that they would not recommend sleeping on until more snow had gone. Popular enough that solitude is not the reason to stop here; proximity to the Bachelor Creek descent is. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: Cub Lake outlet and meadow streams
bivy.capacity: many parties; the meadows absorb a dozen or more groups on a holiday weekend

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes / South Cascade Glacier Col

itinerary: Day 1 (Cascade Pass to Kool-Aid Lake): 4-6 hours, ~3,300 ft gain. Hike Cascade Pass Trail to the pass (3.7 miles), then off-trail south to Cache Col crossing on Cache Glacier, descend to Kool-Aid Lake bivouac (elevation ~6,100 ft). Day 2 (Kool-Aid to Yang-Yang Lakes): 8-11 hours, 2,500 ft gain/loss. Cross the exposed Red Ledge below Art's Knoll (Class 3 scrambling), climb the Middle Cascade Glacier to Spider-Formidable Col, descend to Yang-Yang Lakes bivouac. Day 3 (Yang-Yang to White Rock Lakes): 7-11 hours, 2,000 ft gain/loss. Traverse Le Conte Ridge, cross Le Conte Glacier with crevasse hazards, descend to White Rock Lakes bivouac (visual highlight of entire route). Day 4 (White Rock rest day or peak day): Optional rest day. Dome Peak (8,924 ft) is climbed from the Itswoot Ridge camp instead, via the Dome Glacier route (35-degree snow and ice), as an extra day after Day 5. Day 5 (White Rock to Itswoot Ridge): 8-10 hours, 3,000 ft gain. Ascend Dana Glacier crossing bergschrund, summit Spire Point (8,264 ft) or traverse below on east face, descend to Itswoot Ridge bivouac. Day 6 (Itswoot to Downey Creek TH): 8-12 hours, 2,500 ft loss. Descend Bachelor Creek through forest, reach Downey Creek Trailhead. Alternative faster options: out-and-back from Cascade Pass (4-5 days), or extend to Dome Peak summit and add Sentinel Peak/Old Guard (7-8 days).

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)
White Rock Lakes / South Cascade Glacier Col

name: Ragged Ridge
approach: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, hike the Easy Pass Trail about 3.5 miles and roughly 2,900 ft to Easy Pass, about 6,500 ft. Most parties then leave the trail and sidehill west along the south side of the ridge on grassy benches around 6,600-6,800 ft, crossing many small gullies and buttresses; a large gully with a waterfall just before the basin needs a short descent of steep scree. The usual high camp is in the basin just south of Mesahchie Peak at about 6,600-6,700 ft, roughly five hours from the car. The alternative is to follow the trail down the far side of the pass into the Fisher Creek basin near 5,100 ft and climb off-trail back up to the same camp. From camp, climb northwest to the Mesahchie-Katsuk saddle to start the traverse.
descent: Descend from the ridge to the maintained Fisher Creek trail (rather than sidehilling high back toward Easy Pass) and follow it out over Easy Pass to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: Seasonal and often gone. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

itinerary: Commonly done either as a long single day (~13-14 hrs car-to-car) from Easy Pass, or as a 2-day trip: Day 1 — approach via Easy Pass and Fisher Creek to a high camp (~6,700 ft) on Mesahchie's south shoulder; Day 2 — traverse Mesahchie-Katsuk-Kimtah-Cosho and descend to the Fisher Creek trail.

name: Rampage
approach: Follow the shared Wine Spires trail: boot path down talus to Early Winters Creek, cross on a log, then climb steeply up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the ~6,500 ft basin/camp (roughly 2 hours from the car). For Rampage, keep climbing toward Burgundy Col, then leave the trail rightward across a very loose slope onto a third-class ledge system and follow it right to its far end, where the route's corner begins. A spring near the camp bench is the last reliable water.
descent: Scramble northeast toward Burgundy Spire's North Face and downclimb, or make two 30-meter rappels down the loose gully back to Burgundy Col.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the west side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

itinerary: Most parties climb Rampage alone as a long single day car-to-car, or link it with a Burgundy Spire route (e.g. Action Potential) for a bigger day; one documented Burgundy linkup ran roughly 6 AM to just before 7 PM (~13 hrs) for 12 combined pitches.

waypoints.name: Wine Spires / Silver Star Trailhead (SR-20 MP 166)
Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout

name: Southeast Ridge (Crater Lake Approach)
approach: From Twisp, take Highway 20 south ~2 miles to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to County Rd 1029 (Gold Creek Loop), continuing onto County Rd 1034 (Gold Creek Road), which becomes Forest Road 4340 after about 6 miles. Turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it about 4.6 miles to the Crater Creek Trailhead (~4,750 ft; day-use fee $5, or $30/yr — Northwest Forest Pass/interagency passes accepted). Hike the Crater Creek/Crater Lakes Trail about 3.9 miles one-way, gaining roughly 2,100 ft, to Lower Crater Lake (about 6,840 ft), then continue off-trail up the southeast ridge to the ~8,000 ft col and on to the summit. In late October the spur road to the trailhead was rough but an ordinary car got through; the first stretch of the trail is shared with dirt bikes and is loose and rutted before it turns pleasant.
descent: Reverse the southeast ridge scramble back to the ~8,000 ft col and down into the Crater Lake basin, then out via the Crater Creek Trail.

bivy.name: Crater Lakes, Crater Creek trail
bivy.notes: Lakes at the head of the Crater Creek trail from the Crater Creek trailhead. The natural camp for the southeast ridge; many parties do the route in a day.
bivy.water: Lakes; treat
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Several established sites, best at the upper lake

itinerary: The documented winter ascent (Gilbertson & Robinson, Jan 2019) skied in from an unplowed road to camp at Crater Lake, summited and returned to camp the same day, then skied/hiked out the next day. A summer visit via the maintained Crater Creek/Crater Lakes Trail (7.8 miles round trip to the lake) could reasonably be done as a single long day or a lighter two-day trip with a camp at the lake.

name: Raven Ridge Standard Route (Libby Lake Gully-Ridge)
approach: From Twisp, drive WA-20 east a short distance to WA-153, then south on WA-153 to Libby Creek Road (County Road 1045), about 1.4 miles south of Carlton. Turn right and follow Libby Creek Road about 2.5 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 43 for about 5.1 miles, left onto Forest Road 4340 for about 1.2 miles, right onto Forest Road 4340-700 for about 1.5 miles, and left onto Forest Road 4340-750 for about 0.9 mile to the Libby Lake Trailhead (4,400–4,430 ft; roadside parking for roughly 10 vehicles, no toilet or potable water). From the trailhead, follow Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake, watching for trail damage (root holes) from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire between roughly miles 0.8 and 2.5. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail at about 7,170 ft, used by some parties as a base camp.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent: downclimb the ridge scramble, then carefully downclimb the loose talus gully back to Libby Lake, and return via the Libby Lake Trail to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Libby Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

itinerary: Most parties climb Raven Ridge as a single long day from the Libby Lake Trailhead (roughly 12–13 miles round trip with about 4,200 ft of gain). Parties combining Raven Ridge with Hoodoo Peak often backpack in about 5 miles to camp near the old cabin (~7,170 ft) or at Libby Lake, climb both peaks via the connecting ridge on day two, and hike out on day three (or as a very long single day for fit, fast parties).

name: NW Ridge
approach: From Remmel Lake, bushwhack roughly 2 miles up the forested slope due south of the lake, through mosquito-infested timber and subalpine bog, to a high camp at treeline (~7,500 ft) on the lower NW ridge.
descent: Descend by rappelling the west sides of the two main gendarmes, then scramble down and around the west slope over boulders and scree that range from solid to loose, staying off the north summit route, and walk back to high camp.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. It is also the piece of this zone most likely to be open. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

itinerary: Day 1: Bushwhack from Remmel Lake south through forests and bogs to reach camp at 7,500 feet on lower ridge. Day 2: Climb from camp to summit (3.5 hours typical climbing time from camp), summit and rappel descent back to camp (2.5 hours), return to Remmel Lake.

name: Southeast Slope (Standard Route)
approach: From the Thirtymile Trailhead (end of FR 51, ~3,400 ft) or the Andrews Creek Trailhead (on FR 51 at the end of the pavement, ~3,050 ft), hike into the Pasayten Wilderness. Via Thirtymile: follow the Chewuch River Trail and Four Point Creek Trail to Four Point Lake (6,850 ft), then pick up the abandoned Coleman Ridge Trail; at roughly 7,070 ft a cairn marks the point to leave the trail and climb open meadow/talus up-valley to the summit on a well-trodden unofficial path. Via Andrews Creek: hike the Andrews Creek Trail roughly 9-11 miles (crossing heavy deadfall in an old 2003 burn in the lower miles) to a low saddle between Remmel and Coleman Ridge, then contour the west side of Coleman Ridge to reach the same upper slopes; alternatively continue to Andrews Pass (~6,700 ft) and climb one of several Class 3 west-facing gullies directly to the summit ridge.
descent: Reverse the ascent route on foot back to Four Point Lake/Andrews Pass and out the inbound trailhead.
itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day backpack: Day 1 hike in to camp at Four Point Lake or along the Chewuch/Andrews Creek Trail; Day 2 climb to the summit and return to camp; Day 3 hike out. Strong parties have also completed the whole round trip (25+ miles, 5,500-6,800 ft gain) as a single very long day.

waypoints.name: Unofficial summit trail junction (off abandoned Coleman Ridge Trail)

name: Ridge Traverse from East Fury
approach: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. The Luna Fire closure has shut the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, and bars cross-country travel from the closed trail; check the park's current fire closures before planning.
descent: Traverse back to East Fury summit via the same route (downclimbing towers and using rappels), then descend East Fury via the Southeast Glacier and Class 3 terrain back to Luna Camp and Luna Col, then descend the Access Creek basin to the Big Beaver Trail.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

itinerary: Day 1: Water taxi from Ross Dam to Big Beaver, hike 9.4 miles to Luna Camp. Day 2: Climb Access Creek and Access Col to a high camp at Luna Col. Day 3: From Luna Col, ascend East Fury, traverse to West Fury, and return over East Fury to Luna Col. Day 4: Descend Access Creek and the Big Beaver Trail to Ross Lake for the water taxi return.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) — via Ross Lake water taxi/hike to Big Beaver, then off-trail to Access Creek/Luna Camp

name: Roan Wall - Center Stage
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Rappel the route on its bolted double-ring anchors.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

itinerary: Feasible in a single long day (~3-3.5 hr approach, full 10-pitch climb, rappel descent, ~3-3.5 hr exit), or split by bivying at the Martha's Place boulder near the base the night before to shorten the climbing day. Pairs with Flight of the Falcon on Salish Peak for a big linkup for fast, motivated parties.

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 14-15 miles to the Mazama junction, then turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and drive about 7.5 paved miles and another 1.5 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to Robinson Creek Trailhead (elev. ~2,500-2,560 ft, with an information sign, picnic table, and vault toilet). From the trailhead, hike the Robinson Creek - Middle Fork Trail (#478) north for about 2.8 miles to the signed/bridged Beauty Creek junction (elev. ~3,560 ft) just past a bridge over Beauty Creek. Turn right (northeast/uphill) onto the unmarked, overgrown Beauty Creek Trail and follow it about 1.5 miles up the valley, staying northwest of the creek, to a tributary crossing around 5,200-5,260 ft, then continue up open slopes to the tarn basin at about 6,750-6,800 ft.
descent: Descend the same southeast ridge and scree slope back to the tarn, then retrace the Beauty Creek and Robinson Creek trails to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Beauty Creek tarn camp
bivy.notes: Leave the Robinson Creek trail for the Beauty Creek path, then take the steep boot path up to the tarn below the southeast cirque. The meadows between Robinson and Beauty Peak also have space.
bivy.water: The tarn and its outlet stream.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit.
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites around the tarn.

bivy.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
bivy.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.

itinerary: Commonly done as a very long single day (~14-15 miles round trip, ~6,100-6,500 ft gain, reported car-to-car times around 12 hours) or as an overnight, camping at the Southeast Robinson Tarn (or lower in Beauty Creek valley or at the Robinson Creek bridge) to split the approach and summit push into two days.

name: Northeast Ridge (Nason Ridge Traverse)
approach: Begin at the Old Merritt Lake Trailhead off US-2 (~2,950 ft). Climb via Mahar Creek Ridge to Merritt Lake, then continue over Mt. Mastiff's Southeast Ridge and Mt. Howard's Northeast Ridge (both reported as snow climbs/rock scrambles) before dropping to the Howard-Rock col and climbing Rock Mountain's northeast side.
descent: Descend Rock Mountain's South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin, then exit via the standard Rock Mountain Trail #1587 to the US-2 trailhead.

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about three hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Merritt Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway camp. Its own trail climbs about two thousand feet in two and a half miles from around three thousand feet at the road, which is steep but short by the standards of this ridge, and it is by a wide margin the easiest way to get a loaded pack onto the crest. From here it is three and a half miles west along the ridge trail to Crescent Lake for Howard and Mastiff, and roughly three miles east to Alpine Lookout. That makes it the practical base for the eastern half of the crest and the fallback for anyone who has misjudged the traverse. Lost Lake lies just off the trail nearby and offers quieter lakeside camping if the main camp is full. Mosquitoes here in June are genuinely severe and are the most common complaint about the place. Note that the easternmost nine miles of the ridge trail, from the Lake Wenatchee end out to Alpine Lookout, are open to motorised travel, so the eastern approach is not the quiet walk the western half is.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable all season, and the pivot of the whole ridge's water problem: it is the first water eastbound on a bone-dry trail and there is none whatsoever east of it. Anyone continuing toward Alpine Lookout is carrying every drop from this shore. Treat it; the camp is heavily used.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery, and no parking pass is required at the Merritt Lake trailhead, which is unusual for this stretch of highway and worth not assuming in reverse at the other trailheads. No campfires above 5,000 feet. Use the existing sites and do not pitch on the vegetation, which is thin and slow to recover at a camp this heavily used.
bivy.capacity: A large, well-established camp with a privy — the only toilet anywhere on this ridge — and room for a number of parties. It is the busiest overnight spot on Nason Ridge and gets weekend traffic from hikers who have no interest in the summits at all.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

itinerary: Typically a 2-day, roughly 15-mile traverse: Day 1 - Old Merritt Lake TH to Merritt Lake, over Mt. Mastiff and Mt. Howard to a camp at Upper Canaan Lake Basin (~6,050 ft; ~6,000 ft of cumulative gain to that point). Day 2 - cross the Howard-Rock col, climb Rock Mountain's northeast side, then descend the South Ridge-East Slope past Rock Lake and out the Rock Mountain Trail to the US-2 trailhead (roughly 6,300 ft of cumulative loss over the full traverse). These distance/elevation figures describe the entire 3-peak traverse, not an isolated Rock Mountain ascent.

name: South Ridge Route
approach: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east about 24 miles; just past milepost 130, before crossing the Thunder Arm of Diablo Lake, turn into the south side of Colonial Creek Campground and park in the large lot above the boat ramp. Walk the length of the campground, following signs to the amphitheater, where the Thunder Creek Trail begins. Hike the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 1.7-2.1 miles to the Fourth of July Pass Trail junction, then continue steeply up the west slopes about 5.2 miles total (2,629 ft gain) to Fourth of July Pass.
descent: Descend the same south-ridge route back to Fourth of July Pass and out the Thunder Creek Trail.
itinerary: Day 1: Trailhead to Fourth of July Camp (4.8 mi, ~2,300 ft gain, ~2.7 hrs), set up camp (permanent water source at camp, but none higher on the mountain by mid-summer). Day 2: Camp to summit (~4,000 ft gain, ~6.1 hrs), summit to camp (~3.6 hrs), camp to trailhead (~1.7 hrs). Strong parties can also do it as a single very long day.

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground

name: Scramble Route
approach: The Eagle Peak Trailhead is about 300 feet past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River. From there, a maintained trail (about 7.2 miles round trip, ~2,955 ft gain) climbs steeply through forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky terrain for a final half mile to the 5,700-foot Eagle Peak Saddle, where the maintained trail ends. The saddle is exposed with cliff edges that can be corniced with lingering snow into June; routes onto Eagle Peak itself continue past the saddle as a scramble.
descent: Reverse the route from the summit down to the saddle via Class 3 scrambling (slightly harder on descent—coach teammates through the crux rock step). Descend the trail back to Longmire via the same 3.6-mile switchback trail through forest and meadow.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

itinerary: Typically a single long day trip from Longmire: trailhead to the Eagle Peak-Chutla saddle (~3.6 mi one-way, ~2,900 ft gain), saddle to summit via the ridge scramble (short distance, roughly 250-300 ft of additional gain over uneven terrain), then reverse the full route to the trailhead — on the order of 7-9 miles and ~3,200 ft round trip depending on the exact line taken through the summit scramble.

waypoints.name: Eagle Peak Trailhead (Longmire, Nisqually Suspension Bridge)

name: SE Ridge AKA Shield Wall
approach: From the road-end parking on Forest Road 2419 (off North Lake Cushman Road/FR-24), shared with the standard route, walk the old roadbed past the standard route's trail entrance to just beyond the Big Creek crossing (~3,100 ft); a way trail leads to the base of the southeast ridge's rock section. Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft to a bowl below the Shield Wall; a gully ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's left corner (~4,850 ft) where the technical climbing begins. In late May a steep snow slope sat between the basin and the first bolted pitch; the way trail up to that basin climbs roughly 1,600 ft and is easier to follow than the standard route's trail.
descent: Descend via the standard route rather than reversing the SE Ridge.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

itinerary: Long single day: approach roughly 1-1.25 hrs from the trailhead to the base of the wall, climb 7 pitches (low 5th-5.7) up the Shield Wall, make up to three 30m rappels through the ridge's gendarmes, climb about 6 more pitches (3rd-5.7) to the summit, then descend via the standard route back to the car.

name: Northeast Couloir
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.
descent: Descend the climbing route, or descend around to Sherpa Pass and downclimb from there to camp.

bivy.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
bivy.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
bivy.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
bivy.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

itinerary: Approach from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to a camp in the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut below the couloir; alpine-start to climb the couloir (snow/ice to roughly 50 degrees) to its top, then scramble up and right to the Balanced Rock summit via a short 5.0 pitch; descend the same route or via Sherpa Pass.

name: North Face
approach: Follow the same multi-day approach as the Southwest Route to a high camp on Itswoot Ridge or near the Dome Glacier, then continue over the Dome-Chickamin Glacier col (~8,500 ft) and descend onto the Chickamin Glacier, traversing beneath Sinister's north side to reach the base of the face. The original 1980 first ascent instead approached from the Blizzard-Gunsight col, traversing the Chickamin Glacier from the west. The Downey Creek trail grows muddy, brushy and tangled with deadfall toward Bachelor Creek, then stays rooty and slick for hours until the basin below the ridge.
descent: Descend the Northwest Face/West Ridge line, or reverse the face itself in firm, stable snow conditions, then retrace the glacier approach back to camp.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

itinerary: Follows the same 2-3 day approach to a high camp near Itswoot Ridge/Dome Glacier as the Southwest Route. From high camp, cross to the Dome-Chickamin col, descend onto the Chickamin Glacier, climb the north face directly to the summit, then return to camp and reverse the approach over 1-2 more days.

name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face
approach: From either trailhead, climbers first gain the Pacific Crest Trail — via the Tunnel Creek Trail climbing about 1,170 ft in 1.45 miles to Hope Lake, or via the Surprise Creek Trail to Surprise Lake — then follow the PCT to Trap Pass (~5,800 ft), south from Hope Lake or north from the Surprise Lake side. From Trap Pass an unmaintained climbers' trail continues south along the ridge to the base of Slippery Slab Tower, with Thunder Mountain further along the same ridgeline above Glacier Lake. The round trip is long enough (roughly 6 miles one-way) that many parties camp overnight at Hope Lake or Trap Lake.
descent: Rappel the climbing route using two rappels (60m double-strand or multiple singles). Follow boot path back to Trap Pass and reverse the approach via PCT and Tunnel Creek Trail.

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. No campfires above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

itinerary: Day 1 (if overnight): Depart early morning from Tunnel Creek Trailhead, reach Hope Lake (2-2.5 hrs), continue over Trap Pass and camp at Trap Lake just below it (2-3 additional hours of approach). Day 2: Climb Slippery Slab Tower and return to camp (6-8 hrs). Day 3: Return to trailhead (4-5 hrs). For day trip, depart before dawn and allow 10-12 hours total.
