name: South Face
approach: From the pullout, find a faint boot path descending loose talus/scree to the east into the trees, passing a trail register, then crossing Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft). The trail climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply gaining elevation to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (roughly 2 hours from the car), then continues up to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft, ~3 hours). Vasiliki Tower rises directly from the north side of the col; good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft.
descent: Down climb the North Ridge to return to Burgundy Col or rappel from the summit.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the west side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

itinerary: Commonly done car-to-car in one long day (approach roughly 3-4 hours each way, plus a few hours on route and descent), or split over two days with a bivy at 'The Ledge' (~2 miles in) or at Burgundy Col itself (~7,800 ft) — a good base if linking Vasiliki with Burgundy Spire or other nearby Wine Spires towers.

name: South Face
approach: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 24 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: from Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and climb scree/talus to the base of the peak's main South Face and start low in the centre of the open wall, left of the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk (the SE Buttress starts inside that gully).
descent: Exit west via the standard walk-up (SW slope) descent route.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is burn — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

itinerary: Day 1: drive to trailhead and hike in toward Upper Cathedral Lake basin; Day 2: continue to basecamp if needed and rest/scout; Day 3: climb the South Face car-to-car from camp; Day 4: hike out.

name: South Gully/South Spur
approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
descent: Traverse the ridge from the south summit to the middle summit, rappel roughly 30m from trees to the north summit, then descend west via the Cave Ridge trail to Alpental (or east via the Commonwealth Basin trail) — the standard descent documented for Guye Peak's south-side routes.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

itinerary: A half day in good conditions and most of a day in bad ones. From the Summit West lot in firm winter snow, about an hour of approach up Commonwealth to the base of the gully, then three rope lengths to the first chockstone, a second chockstone and the short ice or rock step above it, and out onto the South Spur to the south summit. If you want the true traverse, continue over the middle summit, make the rappel, and finish up the north summit. Descend west to Alpental or east down Commonwealth. One party in poor conditions - fog to 20 ft visibility, verglas, fresh snow - took most of a day and noted that in good conditions this is a great half-day outing, which is the honest range.

name: South Rib
approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
descent: Traverse north over the subsummits and rappel (via fixed tat) into the Southeast Couloir, then ascend a steep gully to a notch and follow the climbers' trail toward Cave Ridge/Snow Lake.

Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.

itinerary: A half day to a full day, car to car, and a genuinely realistic after-work or short-weather-window objective given the drive from Seattle is under an hour. Park on Alpental Road, walk the ski track and boulder field to the base, and climb five pitches or simulclimb the easier ground. One fit party moving fast on a steep variation of this side of the peak reached the true south summit an hour and a half after leaving the car, which is the low end; a roped party of two on the standard rib should plan on the better part of a day. Descend north over the subsummits and out via the Southeast Couloir and the Cave Ridge trail. No camping needed or wanted.

name: South Ridge
approach: The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route up Bachelor Creek past Cub Lake and over Itswoot Ridge, involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
descent: Do not reverse the ridge. From the summit a rappel of roughly 35 m drops north off the top, and a second rappel takes you east onto the Blue Glacier, which drains the peak's east side. Expect a moat where rock meets ice — parties here have repeatedly found a deep gap at the base, and at least one rappel on this side hung free over it, so plan to land beyond the lip and carry enough cord to leave an anchor. Heading back toward the Chickamin Glacier and the Ptarmigan Traverse camps, cross the south ridge at the first col south of the South Peak; the second col is a common mistake, and one party describes losing time and backtracking after heading there.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

itinerary: Multi-day trip from Stehekin (ferry up Lake Chelan, shuttle to High Bridge) or from Downey Creek in the west; plan 1-2 days of approach, a climbing day, and 1-2 days out.

name: South Ridge
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) to the high camp near 7,600 ft on the Inspiration Glacier flat. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. For this specific route: from high camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline seen from camp, below an obvious crack leading up to a U-shaped notch in the crest.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

itinerary: Day 1: approach to Eldorado high camp (~7,600 ft) via Eldorado Creek and Eldorado Glacier, 5-6 hrs. Day 2: climb the South Ridge (4 pitches) and descend the East Ridge. Day 3: hike out.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH

name: South Ridge
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop, a couple of miles up-road of the Eldorado trailhead, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
descent: Descend the North Ridge: one short rappel from fixed slings, then reverse that ridge.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are no longer free — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Boston Basin trailhead and hike in to high camp (~6,400 ft). Day 2: Early start, approach via snowfields to the base of the South Ridge, climb the 5 pitches to the top, then descend via the North Ridge back to camp.

name: Southeast Ridge (SE Corner)
approach: East-northeast up Shannon Ridge, then traverse Sulphide Glacier to reach southeast ridge base By mid-August one stretch of the forest road to the Shannon Ridge trailhead is washed out and high clearance helps; the trail up the ridge is cleared and easy to follow, and the glacier's lowest slope is hard ice at dawn after a cold night, with crevasses right away and no set bootpack. In mid-June the snow is continuous from about 4,700 ft and the basin camp near 6,200 ft has running water and dry pads; slopes above camp can shed wet avalanches onto the trail on the way out.
descent: Rappel and downclimb the summit pyramid's central gully to the Sulphide Glacier, then reverse the glacier to camp.

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the most straightforward route on Shuksan and the best launching point for the summit pyramid. The plateau is flat, spacious and well positioned, and a privy has been maintained on the ridgeline here in recent seasons, which is unusual at this elevation. The permit is the binding constraint on the whole trip rather than the terrain, so plan the paperwork before the climb. Snow covers the site into early summer, and late in the season the approach turns to loose ground and heather that is harder work than the mileage suggests.
bivy.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a different authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Permits come through Recreation.gov, with a spring early-access lottery followed by a general on-sale, and a share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.
bivy.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there

bivy.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
bivy.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.
bivy.water: Poor. There is essentially nothing between the trailhead streams and the Sulphide Glacier itself, and what does exist on the ridge is gone by late June in most years. Carry water up from the bottom.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the national park boundary — no backcountry permit needed here, which is the entire reason parties use these sites. A recreation pass is required at the Shannon Ridge trailhead. The park boundary is roughly half a mile further up the ridge, and everything beyond it needs a National Park Service permit.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites along the open ridge; adequate but cramped compared to the Sulphide camp above

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
bivy.notes: Some parties carry above the main plateau to shorten summit day to the pyramid, camping on the glacier around 7,500 ft. It is fully exposed, on snow, and above any water, so it only makes sense for a party comfortable with a glacier bivy and a settled forecast. The gain over the lower camp is modest for most people, which is why the 6,400 ft plateau remains the norm. If weather is uncertain, the lower camp is the better place to be.
bivy.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites

itinerary: Typically a 2-3 day trip: Day 1 approach to a bivy near Winnie's Slide or the Sulphide high camp; Day 2 alpine start, cross the glaciers to the Pyramid notch, climb the SE Ridge to the summit, rappel back to the notch; Day 3 (or same day) descend to the trailhead.

name: Southwest Rib
descent: Traverse east over the Westernmost Chessman to reach the Enchantment Plateau, or descend south from Crystal Lake following its outlet stream back down into Crystal Creek Basin.

bivy.name: Crystal Creek basin below the Southwest Rib
bivy.notes: Informal camping on the floor of Crystal Creek basin near the toe of the rib. Reach it by hiking up Crystal Creek from the Ingalls Creek trail, or by dropping south from Crystal Lake on the Enchantment plateau along its outlet stream.
bivy.water: Crystal Creek
bivy.permit: Outside the Enchantment Permit Area once far enough down the basin; self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few informal sites on the basin floor

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Ingalls Creek Trailhead and backpack in via the Ingalls Creek Trail and the Crystal Creek/Nightmare Gorge boot path to a camp in Crystal Creek Basin or at Crystal Lake. Day 2: Climb the Southwest Rib (roughly 19 pitches) to the summit, then descend via the Westernmost Chessman to the Enchantment Plateau or back to Crystal Lake; return to camp. Day 3: Hike out via Crystal Creek and Ingalls Creek Trail to the trailhead.

name: East Face (2002)
approach: When below the east face, scramble up through brush and easy rock to an obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier on the east face.
descent: Not known in detail; parties would descend via the standard west-ridge/southwest-slope route to Lake Elan and out over Headlee Pass.
itinerary: A long day or overnight: the FA party needed 7-8 hours on the route alone and bivied at the summit after arriving in the dark.

name: Upper South Ridge
approach: Approach to Headlee Pass as for the standard route (see that route's approach). Cross the talus toward Vesper/Elan Lake, then take the first ramp heading up and to the right to reach the base of the South Ridge.
descent: Descend via the standard route: down to the west to the Vesper-Sperry saddle, then south back to Headlee Pass and out to the trailhead.
itinerary: Reckon on most of a day - plan for a full day out given the approach to Headlee Pass plus 8 pitches/sections of low-5th climbing and scrambling.

name: Southeast Gully / East Ridge (Spider-Formidable Col)
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft, at the end of the 23.1-mile Cascade River Road from Marblemount), hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (~5,400-5,560 ft). Continue on a climbers' path across talus to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then descend steep snowfields (ice axe/crampons often needed) into the Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,800 ft), a common base camp. From Kool-Aid Lake, cross talus/scree east toward Spider's south face, reach the fringe of the Middle Cascade Glacier (~6,500 ft) after a steep, narrow sidehill traverse, and cross the glacier (crevasses present; rope recommended) to Spider-Formidable Col (~7,320 ft), an alternate, higher base camp used by many climbing parties.
descent: Downclimb the same buttress/gully system back to Spider-Formidable Col (not rappelled), then reverse the Middle Cascade Glacier / Cache Col approach to Cascade Pass and out.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both Spider Mountain and Mount Formidable, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.
bivy.water: The lake and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required; the lake is outside the national park
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on rock and heather benches around the lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: This is the last ground on the park side, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Cascade Pass Trailhead; hike via Cascade Pass and Cache Col to a base camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col (roughly 6-8 miles). Day 2: Climb Spider Mountain via the southeast gully/east ridge (about 3 hours col-to-summit, roughly 8 hours car-to-car equivalent from Kool-Aid Lake); many parties combine it with Mount Formidable from the same camp. Day 3: Hike out to the trailhead.

name: Spontaneity Arete
approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line. In mid-June a patch of avalanche debris lies across the path, and the steeper climbers' trail above has three fixed hand-lines.
descent: Rappel the route (60m rope) or downclimb/descend the loose gully to climber's right.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

itinerary: Pre-dawn/early start from the car; ~1-1.5 hr approach to the base; roughly 4-6 hours for the 6-7 pitches including route-finding and scrambling between belays; 2-3+ hours for the rappel/gully descent back to the creek crossing and pullout — full car-to-car days of 9+ hours are commonly reported.

waypoints.name: SR-20 turnout below Le Petit Cheval (east of Washington Pass)

name: Spontaneous Distraction
approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line.
descent: Rappel the route; a single 70m rope is sufficient.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Same trailhead and trail as the standard scramble: from Twisp, drive Twisp River Road (Co. Rd 9114) west ~10-11 miles, then Buttermilk Creek Rd, East Buttermilk Creek Rd (FR-43), and spur FR-4300-500 to the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead (~3,960 ft). Hike the West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trail about 7 miles and 3,500 ft to 7,480-ft Fish Creek Pass; unlike the standard route, do not descend to Star Lake — instead gain the ridge crest directly above the pass.
descent: The descent off the ridge itself is not documented — no repeat ascent has been recorded — so plan a strategy (downclimb or rappel the ridge, or drop west to the standard Southwest Spur scramble line) before committing above the steep final section. However you get off the summit, the way home is settled: a climbers' trail contours around Point 7,912 and drops to the pass just south of Star Lake, a quarter mile from Fish Creek Pass, where you rejoin the approach. From there retrace the West Fork Buttermilk Creek trail roughly eight miles back to the trailhead. The far side of Fish Creek Pass drains toward Lake Chelan and is not a practical exit.
itinerary: Backpack in via the same trail to a camp at Star Lake or near Fish Creek Pass, then climb the ridge as a technical day trip from camp; allow a full day given the approach length and the ridge's sustained, low-angle length before the crux.

name: Summertime
approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until about midday in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

name: North Face
approach: Approach from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley (North Bend side): drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (NF-56) to its plowed/drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance (about 1 mile in the FA party's case) into the valley. Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing multiple braids of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River (the crux of the approach in high water), then climb to a camp below the north face. The FA party's full approach from vehicle to camp took about 6.5 hours.
descent: Descend the southwest side of the peak via neve slopes, with two 30m rappels down a snow gully back toward the base.
itinerary: Day 1: Drive/bike the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road, hike/ford into the valley and establish camp below the north face (~6.5 hrs). Day 2: Alpine start (~6 AM), climb the ~2,000 ft ice line, descend the SW-side gully with two rappels, and hike back out.
